source1: Donald E. Queller, Thomas F. Madden and Alfred J. Andrea, The Fourth Crusade: The Conquest of Constantinople, University of Pennsylvania Press 1999 - https://books.google.com/books?id=0NpWFGvA5VQC
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Latin Empire of Constantinople, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/place/Latin-Empire-of-Constantinople
notes: Fourth Crusade army and Venetians (external) stormed Constantinople in April 1204 and crowned Baldwin of Flanders Latin emperor. Preceded by coups and depositions (1182, 1185, 1195, 1204) and the Bulgarian revolt. Byzantine rump states survived outside the core.

successor: Holy Roman Empire (continued under Frederick III and Habsburg emperors to 1806)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Holy Roman Empire (800-1806), Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/place/Holy-Roman-Empire
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Frederick III, Holy Roman emperor, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Frederick-III-Holy-Roman-emperor
notes: No break in 1453: imperial institutions continued under Frederick III (German king 1440, emperor 1452-93) until dissolution in 1806; 1453 is a database period boundary. Hussite Wars (1419-34) and noble revolts give Q4 Y.

successor: Mamluk Sultanate (continued; Turkish line to 1382, Circassian to 1517)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Mamluk, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mamluk
source2: none opened (web fetch budget exhausted before a second source could be read)
notes: 1348 (Black Death) is a period boundary; the Mamluk sultanate continued without institutional break (Turkish Mamluks to 1382, Circassian to 1517). Q4 Y: emirs rapidly enthroned and deposed al-Nasir Muhammad's sons after 1341. Q4 detail from background knowledge, unverified online.

successor: British Protectorate of Northern Nigeria (after Royal Niger Company)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Igala, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Igala
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), Nigeria (Wikisource transcription; notes Niger Company treaties with major rulers) - https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nigeria
notes: Royal Niger Company treaty sphere passed to the British Protectorate of Northern Nigeria on 1 Jan 1900; the Attah continued under indirect rule. No conquest of Idah found, but sources thin (web budget exhausted). 19th-century succession disputes weakened Idah.

source1: Victor H. Mair and Prods Oktor Skjaervo, Chinese Turkestan ii. In pre-Islamic times, Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/chinese-turkestan-ii
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Kyrgyzstan: History, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/place/Kyrgyzstan/History
notes: Yenisei Kyrgyz (external) sacked the Orkhon capital in 840 and killed the qaghan, aided by a defecting Uighur minister, after the 839 coup, famine, epidemic and livestock losses. Kyrgyz did not settle Mongolia. Database successor Khitan (907) is too late.

successor: Soomra dynasty of lower Sindh (continued to 1351)
source1: Habibullah Siddiqui, The Soomras of Sindh: their origin, main characteristics and rule (1025-1351 AD), University of Karachi - https://uok.edu.pk/faculties/sindhi/docs/soomroEng.pdf
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Muizz al-Din Muhammad ibn Sam, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Muizz-al-Din-Muhammad-ibn-Sam
notes: Soomra dynasty (capitals Thari, Muhammad Tur) ruled lower Sindh c.1025-1351 across 1193. Ghurids took Multan and Uch 1175 and Debal c.1176-82, but sources disagree on effective control; later Delhi vassalage. The 1193 boundary looks arbitrary.

successor: French Republic (Bonaparte's army; Provisional Municipality), then Habsburg Austria from 1798
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Ludovico Manin, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ludovico-Manin
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Editors), Treaty of Campo Formio, Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Campo-Formio
notes: Under Bonaparte's military pressure the last doge, Manin, was deposed on 12 May 1797 and a provisional municipality replaced the republic under French occupation; Campo Formio (Oct 1797) handed Venice to Austria. Listed candidate successors are wrong.
